en: Then, performing the excellent vow of the teacher, the teacher himself should indeed practice the collection of mantras from Sadyojāta up to Śiva. ||1||

Sleeping on the ground for three fortnights, eating only at night and always subsisting on sacrificial oblations, observing silence, bathing at the three periods of the day, and remaining self-controlled without being agitated by the pairs of opposites; || 2 ||
He should always wear white garments, with white garlands and unguents;
he should carry a yoga-band and a rosary, and wear a girdle of muñja grass and a deerskin.

At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform [the fire sacrifice] according to one's ability and in the proper sequence, using either ghee, or sesame seeds smeared with ghee, or milk, or rice grains. || 4 ||
Either with rice grains, or with sacrificial fuel-sticks, or with curd, or likewise with barley;
or with bilva fruits, or with bilva leaves, or with auspicious flowers fit for sacrifice.
Then, upon the completion of the vow, one should worship the previously mentioned mandala;
at the time of undertaking the vow, both the preceptor and the practitioner [should do so].
Then, having consecrated himself for infinite victory,
the practitioner of mantra should observe the mantra-vow according to the path prescribed for the mantra to be accomplished.
Whether on Pāriyātra, Mahendra, Sahya, or even Malaya;
or on Mantrī, Devagiri, Vindhya, or the Śukti mountain—8.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, or at the ocean, on Śrīśaila or Ṛkṣaparvata, at Arbuda or by a river where it meets the sea of its own accord— 9.
There, he should take up residence in a place endowed with flowers and fruits, auspicious, strewn with earth and kuśa grass, facing east or north, abundant in fuel, and free from noise. (10)

Abiding in that state with a serene mind, one should resort to purification of the body through penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, or by means of subsisting on vegetables and other such prescribed foods. || 11 ||
By restraining the functions of the vital breaths, one should practice the *praṇava* with firm resolve for six months, completing a full hundred thousand repetitions.
On a day augmented by auspicious stars, having purified his body and worshipped the Lord of the gods, he should undertake the ritual of the sesame-clump.
One should resort to a linga endowed with all auspicious marks, which was formerly established by sages, or one that has been consecrated by oneself; for such a linga bestows spiritual perfection.

O Brahmins, one should avoid a linga that is "staked" (kīlita), as well as those associated with Skanda, Viṣṇu, Indra, or the Mothers; likewise, one should avoid a linga placed upon another and a face-linga (mukhaliṅga). 15.
Alternatively, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) endowed with the proper characteristics;
for indeed, the accomplishment of mantras proceeds swiftly even upon such a mound. 16.
The most excellent linga faces west; in its absence, it is prescribed to face east.
However, those facing south or north are not approved by the wise for the attainment of success.
Having taken up the desired auspicious *liṅga* as prescribed in the *Liṅgakalpa*, the practitioner of mantra should worship it constantly, considering the body to be impermanent. 18.
Realizing that it resembles a water bubble, is devoid of divine sovereignty, and is the locus of all sufferings for men, one should attain tranquility. 19.
One should never desire elephants, horses, chariots, or women;
they are like shadows, playthings, or reflections—fleeting causes of bondage.
Such is the nature of unrighteousness that a practitioner might touch a woman;
therefore, having fixed the mind upon the intellect, one should indeed act as impelled by the sacred injunctions. 21.
If he should be drawn away by sense-objects, he should summon nāgas, gandharvas, and yakṣiṇīs with mantras and enjoy them; he should not forcibly touch women of the earth.
If he is afflicted by the objects of the senses, he may enjoy with them for as long as his body remains;
once that body falls away, he attains nirvāṇa.
The practitioner of mantra should not direct even the slightest of his mind toward attachments to music and the like, nor toward other endeavors such as dancing, which are conducive to calamity. (24)
All pure objects of purpose manifest spontaneously for the one who has attained accomplishment;
therefore, having renounced everything else, one should be devoted to the accomplishment of mantra. || 25 ||
The five limbs of the Vidyā are the root of all mantra-siddhis;
therefore, one should practice them first, according to the sequence prescribed in the Kalpa. 26.
Having recited ten million repetitions for each [syllable] according to the path prescribed in the ritual manuals,
and having bathed duly after performing the vows, one should recite the mantra for the sake of attaining perfection.
A wise person should not perform recitation that is delayed, indistinct, uncommitted, or too rapid; nor should it be innumerable or performed with a distracted mind. 28.
Clad in white garments, wearing a white turban, and likewise possessing a white sacred thread,
anointed with white unguents and adorned with garlands, he shall observe the vow of the Lord of Knowledge.
Wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
the practitioner of the mantra should observe the Brahmaśiras vow as previously described for one month.
Wearing yellow garments, with yellow garlands and unguents,
and with a yellow sacred thread, one should observe for a month this supreme vow dedicated to Rudrāṇī.
A wise person, always devoted to the worship of Śiva, should likewise observe this vow for one month even for Indra, the one invoked by many, performing everything with offerings dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
Wearing variegated garments, steadfast, adorned with colorful garlands and unguents,
and devoted to all accomplishments, the practitioner of mantras should observe the Pāśupata vow.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should consecrate oneself with the water of Śiva from a jar,
over which one's own mantra has been recited.

Thus, having bathed according to the vow of knowledge, being authorized in all respects and free from sin, he should then recite the mantra without agitation, according to the procedure of his own ritual manual.
Always keeping the collection of senses well-restrained and never losing his observances,
he should perform the restraint even when there is a lapse, as prescribed by the Vedas for one who is detached.
Brahmins and cows are not to be reviled; nor are those who are embodiments of Śiva, nor the gods, nor the sages, nor the Gaṇas, nor the Mothers.
If one should utter a censure against even one of these,
one should bathe and perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) with all one's heart.
If semen is emitted at night, this very same [penance] minus six [days] is prescribed;
and for sleeping during the day, one should perform the previously mentioned vow with the Aghora mantra.
Having united with a woman while reciting the mantra with the Great Self (the Praṇava),
the practitioner becomes purified by performing one hundred thousand circumambulations while restraining the movement of the vital breaths.

One who has transgressed the vow of knowledge, as well as one who observes the vow of non-undertaking—these two together constitute three times the previous amount, namely one thousand, when properly offered to the teacher. 41.
One who has not been authorized by the mantra should not perform the ritual procedure involving mantras;
if he performs it out of delusion, he must immediately recite the mantra six times, otherwise [the result is lost]. 42.
Using a bed and seat of *kuśa* grass, observing silence, bathing with *kuśa*, drinking *kuśa*-water,
dwelling upon *kuśa*, eating pure food, and reciting mantras, he should practice the vow prescribed by the sacred rules.
If one should, out of delusion, use the discarded floral offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva, he must perform the Brahma-japa one hundred times;
if out of desire, three hundred times, while fasting and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One who possesses pure intellect should perform this very vow three times over;
knowing [the truth], he becomes purified through the infinite sacrifice and the purification of the stages.
But in the case of transgressing any of the other pledges,
one should recite the Elevenfold [Aghora-mantra] for three days while fasting, provided it was done unintentionally.
With his intellect, he should perform the penance according to the gravity of the offense, whether it be measured by the strength of his arms or by the size of the lump of food;
and for those who have committed great sins, having understood their intent, he should prescribe the appropriate expiation.
This is declared to be the supreme atonement for all sins:
one should recite the Ekadaśātman mantra individually or collectively according to the prescribed rite. 48.
One should indeed carry out the words spoken by the teacher as truth without hesitation;
thereby one obtains all fruits, both of this world and the next. 49.

Beginning with a single recitation and continuing up to one hundred thousand repetitions of the eleven-fold mantra of Śiva, this is declared to be the supreme culmination for evildoers in this world. 50.
Therefore, having recognized a transgression, the wise person should perform expiation for the sake of attaining mastery over mantras and for the purpose of worldly enjoyment. 51.

One should constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana); if they are omitted, one should fast for a day. Whether healthy or afflicted by illness, at the conclusion [of the rite], one should mutter the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.

The teacher, having risen by his own will, should indeed perform that same rite three times over when it has been interrupted during the daily observance; he should then mutter the previously mentioned Śiva-mantra.
If there is a lapse regarding many daily rites, that which was declared as a sixfold penance may instead be a thousandfold Soma sacrifice, or even a hundredfold Brahman-sacrifice.
Likewise, fasting, bathing, consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), recitation of mantras,
and burnt offerings destroy the impurity arising from all forms of social intermixture among men.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on Expiation, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
